## My Thinking for This Year

I've been farming these 14 mu for 25 years now, since I was 20. My father taught me, and over the years I've figured out what works on this land. I finished middle school, so I can read the leaflets the extension office puts out, but honestly I trust my own eyes and what my neighbors do more than any pamphlet.

Six people in my household — my wife, my parents, and two kids still in school. That means I need about 1,000 jin of grain for our own consumption, and the rest I sell. With only 14 mu, every decision is about making sure we don't go hungry first, and then maybe earning a little cash. I'm not rich enough to experiment much.

**The wheat:** I plant all 14 mu to winter wheat, same as every year. It's our insurance crop — even if maize fails, we'll have flour. I'll sow around October 12th, when the soil is still warm enough but the autumn rains have come. I buy improved Jimai seed, about 30 jin per mu. I used to save my own seed but the germination got worse year after year.

For fertilizer, the extension guy said 15 kg of nitrogen per mu is enough, but last year I did about that and the wheat looked a bit yellow at jointing. My neighbor Wang applied more and his yield was better. So this year I'll put down a base of compound fertilizer before sowing — about 45 kg per mu of a 16-16-8 blend — and then topdress with urea at green-up in March, maybe 12-13 kg per mu. I know it's a bit more than the book says, but I'd rather waste a little money on fertilizer than lose yield. My family needs to eat.

I'll irrigate three times: once right after planting if it's dry, once at green-up in late March, and once at jointing in April. The well water isn't free — electricity for pumping costs me about 15-20 yuan each time per mu — but wheat without water is a disaster. I'll do flood irrigation, same as everyone.

For chemicals, I'll spray herbicide in early spring when the wheat is still young, and keep an eye out for aphids. If they show up, I'll spray insecticide. Fungicide only if I see powdery mildew — last year I didn't need it.

Harvest will be early June, around the 8th or 10th. I'll hire a combine for the harvest — costs about 50 yuan per mu — because with 14 mu and only my father and me for strong labor, we can't cut it by hand in time. The window to get maize in is too tight.

**The maize:** This is where the pressure is. Wheat comes off June 10th, and I need maize in the ground by June 15th at the latest. I'll rotary till once right after harvest and plant immediately. No time for fancy preparation. I buy hybrid seed every year — it's expensive, about 55 yuan per mu, but the yield difference is obvious. I plant about 3 jin per mu.

For maize fertilizer, I'll put down compound fertilizer at planting — about 40 kg per mu — and then topdress urea when the maize is at the big flare stage, around 10-12 kg per mu. The extension people talk about split applications, but honestly with the time pressure I sometimes wonder if I should just put it all down at once. This year I'll try to do the split — Wang says it makes a difference in dry years.

I'll irrigate twice: once at the 10-leaf stage in mid-July, and once at tasseling in early August. That's the critical window. If it's a wet summer, maybe I skip one, but I can't count on rain anymore.

Herbicide at planting, and I'll watch for armyworm in August — if they come, I spray. Harvest will be late September or early October, depending on the variety.

**Labor and money:** My wife and mother help with fertilizing and irrigation. My father and I do the heavy work. I'll hire 3-4 days of labor for the wheat harvest and another 3-4 days for maize harvest and planting, because those weeks are brutal. Hired labor is 120-150 yuan per day now, so I keep it to a minimum.

My total cash outlay for inputs will be about 6,000 yuan this year. It's a lot for us, but if both crops do okay, I should get 12,000-13,000 yuan in revenue after keeping our food grain. That's how we pay for school fees, medicine, and everything else.
